doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Difficulty of keeping a group together
summary: Hard to find gigs and keep a cohesive group as a sideman; touring tightens a band, as with the Basie rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: I can see how that might make you proud or something. If you had a tune like that and you know once the melody is over and then they launch into their solos, all of a sudden it’s [scats]. And think of the nature of this song when you’re playing. Is it hard — well I think I know the answer to this question but is it hard to find gigs for your own group, keep a cohesive group together?

It is. It is. I mean part of it’s because I don’t do a lot of the business stuff as much as I should. I kind of have a sideman career. Excuse me. But it is hard because you’ve got to play. That’s one of the things back in the day, those guys played all the time, like long

sets, nightly, and tour. You’ve got to work stuff out man. Especially when you get in a band, you get on the road, everything comes together. You know if you’re playing once a week or once every two weeks it’s hard to get continuity with your group. That’s a problem I’m having at least.

Yeah. I have a book, it’s called the Count Basie Bio-discography. These English jazz researchers man, they find this material. And you look at their itinerary. There’s hardly ever a day off, and so that sort of explains why the Great American Rhythm Section, man, they just played so much.
Yeah. Totally. And when you go on a tour with a band and you go out for three weeks or a couple of months, man, yeah, you can see the difference by the end of the tour. It’s really tight.
